    Impact of explicit tracer diffusion schemes over a dispersive tracer advection scheme¶

    Aim of Tutorial¶

    The aim of this tutorial is to dive into the interest of combining a diffusive operator with a dispersive scheme. FCT and UBS methods are examples of schemes where the numerical expression of the methods contains a dispersive term and a diffusive term. Here we choose to deliberately add a diffusive operator to a solely dispersive scheme (CEN) on the saltblock experience to attest of the benefits of having both properties.

    The laplacian smoothes out globally and in an homogenous way the signal, it tends to blur or flatten sharp features quickly (helps with noise). The Bi-laplacian creates gentler transition, smoother curves while preserving overall geometric structure.

    Laplacian is highly efficient at removing high-frequency noise very rapidly and very aggressively. Overtime it leads to a uniform flat average (flat PSD).

    Bi-laplacian diffusion allows a signal to retain its general shape (low frequencies) trends while still eliminating noise (high frequencies).

    Because it minimizes the first derivative (the gradient energy), it forces the data to become as flat as possible, therefore high-magnitude gradients tend to disappear. Gradients are better preserved using bi-laplacian.

    Tracer diffusion for a square wave signal with no advection¶

    In [28]:
    Copied! 
    time_indices = [0, 5, 70, 119]
configs = [
    (lap_test, 'LAP', 'laplacian', '-'),
    (blp_test, 'BLP', 'bi-laplacian', '--')
]


fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 10), sharex=True)


for ax, (data, prefix, diff_type, ls) in zip(axes, configs):

    sliced_data = data.isel(y_grid_T=25, deptht=0)
    

    for t in time_indices:
        ax.plot(sliced_data.isel(time_counter=t), linestyle=ls, label=f'{prefix} t{t}')
    

    ax.plot(ref, color='black', linestyle='-', label='REF', linewidth=1.5)

    ax.set_title(f'Snapshot of the salinity field for a {diff_type} diffusion for a square wave initial distribution')
    ax.set_ylabel('Salinity')
    ax.legend(loc='upper right')
    ax.grid(True, linestyle=':', alpha=0.6)

axes[1].set_xlabel('X index')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

    Bi-laplacian diffusion can overshoots and undershoots near sharp edges contrary to laplacian diffusion.

    Maximum & minimum values of the salinity field for the Bi-laplacian¶

    overshoot = []
undershoot = []
MID =[]
print(blp_test.shape)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1,3, figsize=(12,4))
for t in range (blp_test.shape[0]):
    max = blp_test.isel(deptht=0, time_counter=t, y_grid_T = 25).max()
    min = blp_test.isel(deptht=0, time_counter=t, y_grid_T = 25).min()
    mid = blp_test.isel(deptht=0, time_counter=t, x_grid_T = 25, y_grid_T = 25)

    undershoot.append(min)
